tells: 'The reward.' - a verbless label used as a sentence; Author A never writes fragment headings inside prose and would lead with a full sentence such as 'The first gift is nearness.'
'in the lecturer's reading' - Author A always names the speaker ('Sheikh Bahmanpour', 'the Sheikh') and never calls him 'the lecturer'

'The second gift is a different kind of life.' placed bare before the verse - Author A introduces a verse by saying where it comes from and what it does ('The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse'); here the verse arrives without its surah or context

'pure of the filth of this world ... rise above the concerns that infect everyone else' / 'is of course what mystics are after' - the imagery is more coloured and the phrasing more spoken than Author A's plain, measured diction

'is about something else: catching the signs of Allah: becoming sensitive to them' - two colons stacked in one clause; Author A uses one colon per sentence and would write 'Islamic mysticism is about catching the signs of Allah: becoming sensitive to them...'
'Pursuing it means training the soul' - opens on a bare pronoun with no antecedent in the passage; Author A names the subject ('Pursuing ʿirfan')
'and he does not soften it' - an editorial flourish added to close the paragraph; Author A stops once the term is glossed ('is the gravest charge in Islam')
'His closing words to his first class were stronger' - a roundabout, slightly dramatised linking line; Author A links with a plain statement ('He ended his first lecture more strongly')

Opens the chapter the way Author A does, with a familiar devotional occasion ('On Fridays many of us read...', compare the weddings verse and the Munajat), then frames the chapter's question in plain declaratives and points back to an earlier chapter

Each paragraph opens by taking up the last ('Where such a teacher stands is set out by ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi'), short glosses ('a murid, a disciple') and the comma dropped before 'and' as in the reference

'Each step of this chapter has led here.' followed by a whole recap paragraph - Author A does not sum up the chapter at its end; the reference chapter closes on a new point ('Repair is only the start')
'ʿIrfan, then, is worth pursuing: it is the training of the soul...' - a tidy concluding line built on 'then' and a colon; Author A avoids aphoristic summary sentences

'ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi's definition says the same thing: "The real gnostic is..."' - claim, colon and quotation, with the quotation left unexplained; Author A introduces a quotation inside a sentence and then speaks to it
'the two things by which the friends of God fly' - a lyrical turn; Author A's register is plainer

Each verse is introduced by its source and its role ('Surah Fatir describes the same people by what they feel'), the reading is credited to Sheikh Bahmanpour, and the sentences are short contrasts, as in the reference ('Most of us fear Allah's punishment. The people of this verse...')

Introduces Mutahhari's quotation inside the sentence and then explains it ('Mutahhari explains why seeking them would be so: the goal has become something other than God'); plain linking, as in the reference's handling of Tabatabaʾi and Shomali

Names the subject outright ('Pursuing ʿirfan'), credits the reading to Sheikh Bahmanpour in a plain declarative, uses one colon per sentence and ends on a gloss rather than a comment, all matching the reference

'But our knowledge of tawhid...' and 'And Surah Yunus gives them a second name' - sentences opened with 'But' and 'And'; Author A links with full statements and would write 'Our knowledge of tawhid... is still not...'
'Surah Fatir adds: "Only those of Allah's servants having knowledge fear Him".' - claim, colon and quotation run inline; Author A introduces the surah's point in a sentence and sets the verse apart
'which the lectures treat as the same people' - credits 'the lectures' rather than the speaker; Author A writes 'Sheikh Bahmanpour treats'
'fear Him, with a fear that is not about punishment' - the comma adds a pause for effect, which Author A's plain punctuation does not do

Links back plainly ('Tabatabaʾi gives a test for that case too'), brings in the quotation within the sentence and draws the consequence from it, and sets up the next quotation with a sourced lead-in ('recorded in Lantern of the Path, the book attributed to Imam al-Sadiq (as)')

Points back to earlier chapters in plain terms, glosses terms briefly ('wusul, the goal of the road'; 'a wali, a friend of God') and closes on two short contrasting declaratives, like the reference's 'God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them'

Introduces the verse by its surah and its promise ('promised in Surah al-Nahl to whoever acts righteously'), names Sheikh Bahmanpour rather than 'the lecturer', and uses plain, measured diction ('without being soiled by it')
